questions.title: Why is an evolutionary search necessary if YaRN already handles non-uniformities?
questions.question_body: I am reading the LongRoPE paper and I understand that YaRN already divides RoPE dimensions into three frequency-based groups to apply different interpolation strategies (extrapolation, NTK, and linear). The paper argues that LongRoPE identifies 'subtle non-uniformity' that YaRN misses. Could someone explain conceptually what these 'subtle' non-uniformities are? If YaRN is already grouping frequencies to handle different behaviors, why is a custom search for each individual dimension $\lambda_i$ significantly better?

questions.title: How does the piecewise function $\mathbb{I}(\hat{\lambda}_{i}, \hat{n})$ differ from standard Position Interpolation (PI)?
questions.question_body: In Equation 3, the authors define a rescaling factor $\mathbb{I}(\hat{\lambda}_{i}, \hat{n})$ that depends on the token position $n$ and a threshold $\hat{n}$. In standard Position Interpolation (PI), the rescaling factor is a constant $s$ applied to all positions. Could someone explain the intuition behind why keeping the first $\hat{n}$ tokens without interpolation (where the factor is 1) improves performance? Why do these specific initial tokens need to be 'preserved'?

questions.title: What is the intuition behind the 'progressive extension' strategy instead of direct 2048k fine-tuning?
questions.question_body: The paper proposes a strategy where they first search and fine-tune for 256k, and then perform a second search to reach 2048k. Why is this two-step process preferred over simply searching for the optimal RoPE factors for 2048k directly and then fine-tuning the model on the 2048k data? Does the paper provide a specific reason why direct fine-tuning at such a high extension ratio ($512\times$) is 'challenging' for the model's weights?

questions.title: How does the monotonicity constraint $\lambda_i \le \lambda_{i+1}$ relate to NTK theory?
questions.question_body: In the search algorithm (Section 3.2), the authors impose a constraint that the rescale factors $\lambda_i$ must be non-decreasing as the dimension $i$ increases. The paper mentions this is based on NTK theory, suggesting that lower dimensions (higher frequencies) require less interpolation (smaller $\lambda_i$) and higher dimensions (lower frequencies) can handle more (larger $\lambda_i$). I'm struggling to understand the mathematical link: why does a higher frequency dimension specifically require a smaller $\lambda_i$ to maintain the model's ability to distinguish between positions?

questions.title: Does 'Short Context Window Recovery' involve updating the model weights or just the RoPE calculation?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.3, the authors describe 'readjusting' the RoPE rescale factors to recover performance on 4k and 8k contexts after extending the model to 2048k. During inference, if the sequence length is less than 8k, the paper says they 'update RoPE with the searched rescale factors.' Does this mean the model's weights remain frozen and we are only changing the rotation angles calculated on the fly, or does this recovery step involve a new round of gradient descent?

questions.title: How does the 'crowding' effect physically manifest in the attention mechanism?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that standard Position Interpolation (PI) makes position information 'crowded,' which hinders the model's ability to distinguish between closely positioned tokens. Could someone explain the mechanics of this? If we downscale the rotation angles $\theta_i$ by a large factor $s$, how does that specifically lead to the attention mechanism 'confusing' two adjacent tokens? Is it a matter of the dot-product similarity becoming too uniform?
